name: Business Requirements Document
description: Business Requirements Document — single-source template (edit this file to tune). Section/sub-section instructions state the FORMAT, exact table COLUMNS and an EXAMPLE, aligned to the reference AESL Drishti BRD.
system_instructions: You are a senior business analyst writing a formal Business Requirements Document for Adani Energy Solutions Limited (AESL). Professional, precise, third-person business English. Be specific — pull real names, numbers, systems, dates and figures from the source material; never use vague placeholders. Each section must ADD new information — do not repeat content from other sections. Honour the 'MUST NOT INCLUDE' scope boundary supplied with each section. For table sections output a valid GitHub-flavoured Markdown pipe table with a header row and a separator row, using EXACTLY the columns named in the section spec. Do not use emoji.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.instructions:
**Format:** 3 short prose paragraphs (no bullets, no table).
Answer WHAT the project is and WHY the business needs it. Paragraph 1 - purpose of the project. Paragraph 2 - business context and current challenges. Paragraph 3 - expected outcomes with measurable targets. Business-context only ('elevator pitch').
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: technical architecture, tool/technology names, regulatory clauses (unless user brief explicitly requires), implementation approach, cost details, timeline. This section is business-context ONLY.
sections.remarks: Use user input only for actual content. Keep it 3-5 paragraphs.

sections.title: Scope
sections.instructions:
**Format:** one 2-line opening sentence, then TWO bulleted lists under bold sub-headings **In Scope** and **Out of Scope** (no table).
In-Scope bullets cover: problem focus, lifecycle stages, coverage & scale (with numbers), in-scope systems/integrations, operational deliverables, and rules/criteria. Out-of-Scope: 4-6 bullets each with a brief reason.
**Example:** `- Ingestion of SAP ECC and non-SAP sources into the lakehouse (Bronze layer).`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: detailed technical architecture (that goes in Solution Overview), regulatory clauses (unless project is regulatory), cost breakdown, resource plan, vendor names.
sections.remarks: Mention in-scope and out-of-scope clearly. Use bullets for clarity.

sections.title: Terms and Definition
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY two columns: `Terms | Definition`.
List 15-20 project-specific terms that actually appear in THIS BRD, sorted alphabetically, each with a one-line plain-English meaning. Pick only project-relevant terms.
**Example row:** `| SCADA | Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition - real-time grid control system. |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: universally-known terms (API, KPI, SLA, UAT), terms not appearing in this BRD, generic industry abbreviations. Do NOT list all 547 ontology terms — only project-relevant ones.
sections.remarks: Two-column table: Term | Definition. Include domain-specific terms.

sections.title: Business Requirements Summary
sections.instructions:
Generate Section "Business Requirements Summary" together with ALL of its sub-sections below, as ONE continuous block. Begin with a brief 2-3 line high-level intro for the parent (current situation, vision, measurable goals, solution direction), then write EACH sub-section in order under its OWN Markdown heading exactly as shown - do not merge, skip, or reorder sub-sections.

SUB-SECTIONS:

## 4.1 Business Need and Why?
  - **Format:** 3 prose paragraphs.
  - Write: (1) what business capability is needed and by whom, (2) strategic rationale, (3) urgency and consequence of inaction. Business framing only.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: technical solution details, competitor references.

## 4.2 Context for Business Need
  - **Format:** 2-3 prose paragraphs.
  - Write: the current landscape that makes this project necessary - current-state challenges, business context, organizational readiness. Do not repeat 4.1.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: technical architecture, cost/timeline, competitor names.

## 4.3 Problem Statement
  - **Format:** 2-4 short prose paragraphs, one per problem dimension, using the framing 'From [current problem state] -> To [target future state]'.
  - Write: the core problems only (process gaps, data gaps, control gaps, value gaps).
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: solutions, tools, or technology.
  - **Example:** 'From fragmented reports across 6 systems -> To a single governed source of truth.'

## 4.4 Business Value Delivered
  - **Format:** bulleted list of 8-12 items, each `[✓] Category (value type): quantified benefit`.
  - Write: measurable benefits by category (Cost savings, Efficiency, Risk mitigation, Compliance, Engagement, Data quality, Strategic optionality) with numbers.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: technical benefits, unquantified fluffy claims.
  - **Example:** `- [✓] Efficiency: 40% reduction in manual reconciliation (~2,000 hrs/yr).`

## 4.5 Competitor Landscape and Positioning
  - **Format:** ONE 3-4 line intro paragraph only (parent framing).
  - Write: what type of solutions exist in the market for this problem domain.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: specific competitor names / tool comparisons / positioning claims (those are 4.5.1-4.5.3).

### 4.5.1 Competitor Landscape
  - **Format:** bulleted list of 4-6 items.
  - Write each: `Competitor Name (Region) - Product/Approach; Maturity: [Early/Emerging/Mature]; Benchmark: [metric]`. India first, then 1-2 global.
  - **Example:** `- Acme Data (India) - lakehouse services; Maturity: Emerging; Benchmark: 30+ utility clients.`

### 4.5.2 Similar Digital Solutions
  - **Format:** bulleted list of 4-6 items.
  - Write each: `Solution Category (example tools) - Strengths; how this project differentiates`.
  - **Example:** `- Data Lakehouse platforms (Databricks, Synapse) - unified batch/stream; we add utility-domain governance.`

### 4.5.3 Positioning
  - **Format:** 2 prose paragraphs.
  - Write: (1) organizational assets/capabilities that uniquely enable this project; (2) strategic differentiation and expected impact.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: competitor names, tool names.

## 4.6 Critical Success Factors
  - **Format:** bulleted list of 6-9 items.
  - Write each: `Factor Title - what success looks like. Ownership: [Role/Dept]`. Cover Sponsorship, Governance, Data Quality, Integration Readiness, Adoption, Compliance, Stakeholder alignment.
  - **Example:** `- Executive Sponsorship - sustained CXO ownership and funding. Ownership: Business Head.`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: technical architecture details, tool names, functional requirement tables, regulatory clauses. Sub-sections 4.1-4.6 will detail the aspects.
sections.variables: Business Need, Problem Statement, Vision, Goals, Proposed Solution
sections.remarks: Executive-style summary. Parent section — keep high-level. Details follow in 4.1–4.6.

sections.title: Business Process
sections.instructions:
Generate Section "Business Process" together with ALL of its sub-sections below, as ONE continuous block. Begin with a brief parent intro, then write EACH sub-section in order under its OWN Markdown heading exactly as shown - do not merge, skip, or reorder sub-sections.

PARENT INTRO (5 Business Process) - **Format:** 1 short paragraph (3-4 lines) + 6-10 numbered lifecycle steps, each `Step Name - brief description; System/Tool used`.

SUB-SECTIONS:

## 5.1 Pain Areas or Opportunities in Existing Operational Process
  - **Format:** bulleted list of 7-10 items.
  - Write each: `Category - description of the operational pain. Opportunity: what this project could solve`. Cover manual effort, data quality, governance, auditability, reporting, efficiency.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: technology pain (that is 5.2).

## 5.2 Pain Areas or Opportunities in Existing Technology/Systems
  - **Format:** bulleted list of 5-8 items.
  - Write each: `System/Category - specific technical pain. Impact: business consequence`. Reference actual systems from the technical landscape that have gaps for this use case.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: operational/process pain (that is 5.1).

## 5.3 Business Functionality Impact
  - **Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 4 columns: `Department/System | Current State | Future State (Post-Implementation) | Impact/Benefit` (8-10 rows).
  - Write: how each impacted department/system's way of working changes after the project.
  - **Example row:** `| Billing | Manual monthly reconciliation | Automated daily reconciliation | 90% less effort, fewer disputes |`

## 5.4 Business Process Impacted
  - **Format:** 1 short paragraph (parent framing) identifying which business processes are impacted.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: detailed steps (those are 5.4.1 and 5.4.2).

### 5.4.1 As-Is Business Process
  - **Format:** TWO parts - (a) a brief narrative describing how the process works TODAY and the gaps/inefficiencies; THEN (b) a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 4 columns: `Process_id | Process Name | Current Steps | Average Time (days/hours)`.
  - Write: list each current business process as a row - its ID, name, the current steps performed, and the AVERAGE TIME each process takes today (state in days or hours).
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: proposed improvements (that is 5.4.2), cost.
  - **Example table:**
    `| Process_id | Process Name | Current Steps | Average Time (days/hours) |`
    `| PR-01 | Monthly Data Reconciliation | Manually export from SAP IS-U, SCADA & GIS and reconcile in Excel | ~5 days |`

### 5.4.2 To-Be Business Process (New/Changes Only)
  - **Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 5 columns: `PR ID | Process Name | To-Be Description | Change Type | Enabling Systems` (10-18 rows). Change Type is one of New/Enhanced/Automated.
  - Write: only the NEW or CHANGED processes and the value each delivers.
  - MUST NOT INCLUDE: current-state description (that is 5.4.1).
  - **Example row:** `| PR-01 | Data Reconciliation | Auto-reconcile across sources nightly | Automated | Databricks, SAP IS-U |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: detailed AS-IS process (goes in 5.4.1), TO-BE detail (goes in 5.4.2), technology architecture. Focus is the lifecycle ORCHESTRATION view.
sections.variables: Current Process, Data Landscape, Operational Context
sections.remarks: Overview paragraph. Detailed pain areas and process impacts follow in sub-sections.

sections.title: Business Use Cases
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 8 columns: `Use case # | Name | Trigger event | Primary actor | Secondary actor | Main action | Expected outcome | Exception`.
List 10-15 business use cases covering the full lifecycle of THIS project's domain, in plain business terms (what users want to ACHIEVE). Keep each cell crisp (max ~10-15 words).
**Example row:** `| UC-01 | Onboard data source | New source system identified | Data Engineer | Data Steward | Configure & validate ingestion pipeline | Source data available in Bronze layer | Source schema unavailable |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: technical use cases (implementation-level scenarios), infrastructure use cases (backup/monitoring), regulatory use cases (unless project is regulatory). Focus on BUSINESS-USER-FACING scenarios.
sections.variables: Use case # | Name | Trigger event | Primary actor | Secondary actor | Main action | Expected outcome | Exception
sections.remarks: Generate UC1, UC2 etc. from input. Table cells must be crisp — max 10-15 words per cell.

sections.title: Business Requirements
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 5 columns: `Req# | Description | Rationale | Impacted Stakeholder | Remarks`.
List 15-20 business requirements (WHAT the business needs, not how it is built), grouped logically (e.g. Ingestion, Governance, Reporting). Use IDs like `BRQ-001` in Req#. Every requirement should trace to at least one Business Use Case. Use real stakeholder names from the brief. Keep cells short and crisp.
**Example row:** `| BRQ-001 | The platform shall provide a single governed data catalogue. | Eliminates duplicate, conflicting reports. | Data Office, BU Heads | Traceable to UC-03 |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: implementation details (belongs in FRs), NFRs, technical specifications. Focus is BUSINESS CAPABILITY requirements — what business needs the system to do.
sections.variables: Req# | Description | Rationale | Impacted Stakeholder | Remarks
sections.remarks: Requirement IDs like BRQ-001. Table cells must be short and crisp. Scale based on complexity.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 6 columns: `Req# | FR | Description | Rationale | Impacted Stakeholder | Remarks`.
List 20-25 functional requirements (specific system features/behaviours). Req# links to the parent BRQ; FR is the functional-requirement ID (e.g. `FR-001`). Each FR = one testable system behaviour. Keep the FR->BRQ link in every row. Cells short and scannable.
**Example row:** `| BRQ-001 | FR-001 | System shall auto-detect source schema changes and alert stewards. | Prevents pipeline breakage. | Data Engineering | Batch + streaming |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: NFRs (quality attributes), business rules (BRQ level), infrastructure requirements. Focus is SYSTEM FEATURES — what the system does, function by function.
sections.variables: Req# | FR | Description | Rationale | Impacted Stakeholder | Remarks
sections.remarks: Requirement IDs like FR-001. Link to parent BRQ. Table cells must be short and scannable.

sections.title: Non-Functional Requirements
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 6 columns: `Req# | NFR | Description | Rationale | Impacted Stakeholder | Remarks`.
List 18-25 NFRs (quality attributes with measurable targets), grouped by category: Performance, Scalability, Availability, Security, Privacy, Compliance, Backup/DR, Observability, Maintainability, Usability, AI Safety (if AI). NFR is the ID (e.g. `NFR-001`); Req# links to the parent BRQ where applicable.
**Example row:** `| BRQ-004 | NFR-001 | Dashboards shall load in <5 seconds for 500 concurrent users. | User adoption. | Operations, BU users | Peak-load target |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: functional features (that's FRs), business rules, cost NFRs. Focus is QUALITY ATTRIBUTES with measurable targets.
sections.variables: Req# | NFR | Description | Rationale | Impacted Stakeholder | Remarks
sections.remarks: Include NFR constraints from project input. Group by category: Performance, Security, Availability, etc.

sections.title: Solution Overview - Cloud First Approach
sections.instructions:
**Format:** 6-8 bullets, one per architectural layer (prose bullets, optional layer sub-headings; no requirements table).
Cover: Hosting/Infrastructure, Ingestion, Data Storage (Bronze/Silver/Gold), Processing/Orchestration, AI/Analytics, Dev Stack & CI/CD, Security/Integrations, Monitoring/Operations. Name real tools from the technical landscape but mark them 'candidates subject to architecture approval'.
**Example:** `- Data Storage: medallion lakehouse on ADLS Gen2 + Delta (Bronze/Silver/Gold) - candidate.`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: business context (already covered), specific vendor pricing, deployment schedule (that's Section 12). Focus is TECHNICAL ARCHITECTURE at candidate level.
sections.variables: Cloud Platform, Data Ingestion, Bronze/Silver/Gold, Processing Engine, Infrastructure, Algorithms/AI, CI/CD
sections.remarks: Applicable for cloud/data/AI projects. Include architecture narrative and tech stack details.

sections.title: Key Constraints
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a bulleted list of 6-10 constraints grouped by category (no table).
Categories: Performance, Security, Operational, Installation/Deployment, Procedural/Governance, Flexibility, Compatibility. One line per constraint.
**Example:** `- Security: all data at rest must be encrypted (AES-256) and access RBAC-governed.`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: assumptions (that's Section 13), risks, resource limitations. Focus is DELIVERY-BINDING CONSTRAINTS — what must be true.
sections.variables: Performance, Security, Operational, Installation, Procedural, Flexibility, Compatibility
sections.remarks: Bullet list with brief description per constraint category.

sections.title: Project Schedule
sections.instructions:
**Format:** one intro line, then a Markdown table with EXACTLY these 4 columns: `Stage | Gate | Planned Date | Remarks` (only 5-7 rows).
Use the AESL standard gates: PI Gate, PC Gate, VR Gate, UATR Gate, RO Gate, PCD Gate. Durations should reflect the brief's timeline.
**Example row:** `| Design | PC Gate | Week 4-6 | Solution architecture approved |`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: detailed WBS (belongs in project plan), resource assignments, cost per stage. Focus is HIGH-LEVEL GATE-BASED SCHEDULE only.
sections.remarks: Dates can be tentative. Table: Stage | Gate | Planned Date | Remarks

sections.title: Other Constraints and Assumptions If Any
sections.instructions:
**Format:** a bulleted list of 8-15 assumptions/soft-constraints (no table).
Format each: `Category - Description. Owner: [Role/Team if known]`. Cover: IT Infrastructure, Identity/Access, Integrations, Governance, GenAI Guardrails (if AI), Data Residency, Approvals, Support Readiness, DR/Backup, UAT Participation.
**Example:** `- Identity/Access: SSO via Azure AD assumed available at project start. Owner: IT Security.`
sections.scope_boundary: EXCLUDE: hard constraints (that's Section 11), risks (separate section if needed), cost analysis. Focus is ASSUMPTIONS + SOFT CONSTRAINTS that support delivery.
sections.remarks: Include IT support, infra, approval dependencies. Keep concise.
